facts.statement: The genus Bandringa was described in 1969 by the paleontologist Rainer Zangerl.
facts.quote: The genus was described in 1969 by paleontologist Rainer Zangerl

facts.statement: The holotype specimen, a juvenile found in an ironstone concretion in Illinois, was discovered in the summer of 1967.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, FMNH PF 5686, is a juvenile individual which was found in an ironstone concretion in Illinois during the summer of 1967

facts.statement: The genus and species were named after Ray Bandringa, who discovered the holotype specimen.
facts.quote: This specimen was found by Ray Bandringa, to whom the genus and species owe their name

facts.statement: Because all Mazon Creek individuals appear to be juveniles, researchers suggest the area may have served as a nursery.
facts.quote: All Mazon Creek individuals appear to represent juveniles, suggesting the area was a nursery for them

facts.statement: Bandringa lived during the Pennsylvanian subperiod of the Carboniferous period.
facts.quote: Bandringa is an extinct genus of elasmobranch known from the Pennsylvanian subperiod of the Carboniferous period

facts.statement: Bandringa lived between 315.2 and 307 million years ago during the Moscovian age.
facts.quote: Time range: Moscovian to Moscovian (315.2 to 307 million years ago)

facts.statement: Bandringa had a very long snout that made up half of its total body length.
facts.quote: The most noticeable part of this elasmobranch is its very long snout, which made up half of its body

facts.statement: The body of Bandringa featured two dorsal fins, three anal fins, and a long tapering heterocercal tail fin.
facts.quote: The body of Bandringa had two dorsal fins, a set of three anal fins (5 in total) and a long tapering Heterocercal caudal fin

facts.statement: Bandringa likely used suction feeding and its long snout with needle-like cheek spines to hunt in murky water.
facts.quote: It appears to have fed via suction feeding, and used its long snout and needle like spines on its cheek for hunting in murky water

facts.statement: Preserved gut contents of Bandringa include articulated arthropods.
facts.quote: Preserved gut contents include articulated arthropods

facts.statement: Research suggests Bandringa had a life cycle opposite to salmon, with adults living in freshwater and juveniles in brackish or saltwater areas.
facts.quote: Sallan and coauthors in 2014 found that the fish lived a lifestyle that was the opposite of salmon, with the adults living in freshwater areas and the younger ones living in more brackish and saltwater areas

facts.statement: Bandringa is a monotypic genus containing only one known species, B. rayi, which forms the sole member of the family Bandringidae.
facts.quote: There is currently a single known species, B. rayi, which constitutes the sole member of the monotypic family Bandringidae

facts.statement: Bandringa is classified within the class Chondrichthyes.
It is currently unclear how Bandringa relates to other elasmobranchs, though it was originally thought to be an aberrant member of the order Ctenacanthiformes.
facts.quote: While Bandringa was originally described as an aberrant member of the order Ctenacanthiformes, its relationships to other elasmobranchs is currently unclear
